subtype: Approach: seeking help when control keeps failing [Revision]
passage:
Weeks one to four. Yash tried everything: app limits, the phone on the hall shelf, if-then cards. Each plan worked for a few days. Then he was scrolling till two in the morning again. His marks slid from seventy-two to fifty-eight. He felt ashamed and told nobody.
Week five. After a bad exam he said to his mother, “I've tried and I can't stop.” She didn't scold. The next morning they both went to see Trisha ma'am, the school counsellor.
Two weeks later. Trisha ma'am had set up a structured routine with Yash, with fixed wind-down time and a weekly check-in. “If it keeps going or worries you, we can look at more support together,” she said. That night Yash was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: Who did Yash speak to, with his parent?
How did Yash feel after several failed plans?
qa.a: Ashamed and frustrated: he told nobody and only spoke after a bad exam.

qa.q: What else could Yash do if the routine is not enough, and why?
qa.a: Tell the counsellor and his parents so they can look at more support, since needing more help is a sign to ask, not a failure.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Trisha ma'am?
qa.a: Trisha ma'am sees a student who kept trying and then asked for help, and can offer a routine and follow-up with his parents without blame.

grounding: Despite several plans, a teen still loses sleep and grades, and speaks to a school counsellor with a parent.
